title: 7. Strategic Recommendations for Academic Libraries
text:
Actionable Recommendations

1. Adopt an Explicit, Multi-Dimensional Definition of AI Literacy
Move beyond implicit operationalization. Libraries should formally adopt a multi-dimensional definition (such as Leo Lo’s taxonomy or UCSB’s three-stage continuum: Understand, Use and Apply, Analyze and Evaluate) that explicitly connects AI literacy to information literacy, digital ethics, and cognitive development.


2. Update Source Evaluation Rubrics for Generative Media
Traditional source evaluation rubrics (such as the CRAAP test) presuppose human authorship, peer review, and stable publication channels. Libraries should implement evaluation rubrics tailored to generative systems—such as The ROBOT Test (Reliability, Objective, Bias, Owner, Type)—and train students in Lateral Reading to independently corroborate non-deterministic outputs and synthetic citations.


3. Integrate Structured Prompt Engineering into Information Literacy
Incorporate structured prompting heuristics (CLEAR, RTF, TAG, Conversational Threading) into library instruction. Reframing prompt design as strategic, iterative query formulation reinforces core information literacy concepts: faceted search, parameter manipulation, and context setting.


4. Teach Sociotechnical, Environmental, and Labor Dimensions
Following the models of UC Irvine, Chapman, and UC Merced, expand curricula beyond functional mechanics to examine the material impacts of GenAI: - Ecological Footprints: The substantial electrical energy and cooling water requirements of enterprise AI data centers. - Data Labor Supply Chains: The outsourced, low-wage human labor involved in data labeling, cleaning, and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). - Algorithmic Bias & Representation: The systemic cultural, demographic, and epistemological skews embedded in massive web-scraped training datasets.


5. Partner with Campus Teaching Centers on Authentic Assessment
Collaborate closely with campus Centers for Teaching and Learning (modeled by UC Davis and USC) to support faculty in assignment redesign. Libraries should guide instructors toward process-oriented, authentic assessments that emphasize metacognitive reflection, research defense, and peer review (e.g., the PAIR/PAIRR framework), mitigating uncritical cognitive offloading while fostering genuine intellectual agency.

section: 1. Adapting the ACRL Framework for Information Literacy
text:
1. Adapting the ACRL Framework for Information Literacy
The ACRL Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education provides the primary theoretical grounding across research libraries (e.g., UC Irvine, USC, UC Davis):

Authority Is Constructed and Contextual: GenAI systems generate fluent, syntactically flawless text that creates an illusion of expertise. Libraries teach that fluency \(\neq\) factual validity, requiring students to interrogate the underlying data provenance and epistemic grounding of algorithmic responses.
Information Creation as a Process: Generative models obscure the research, editing, and labor processes behind text creation. Students are taught to investigate the hidden training pipelines, web-scraping practices, and human moderation labor (RLHF) that shape model behaviors.
Searching as Strategic Exploration: Traditional boolean keyword retrieval is contrasted with probabilistic natural language interaction. Searching evolves from index querying into conversational negotiation and iterative refinement.

2. Evaluation Rubrics: The ROBOT Test
Originating from Hervieux & Wheatley (2020) and featured prominently in UC Davis and William & Mary guides, the ROBOT Test replaces the traditional CRAAP test to evaluate generative, synthetic outputs:

    A["R - Reliability
Fact-check claims against verified primary literature"] --> B["O - Objective
Identify developer motives and commercial interests"]

Interrogate model outputs for cultural and training skew"]
    C --> D["O - Ownership

    D --> E["T - Type
Distinguish predictive LLM vs specialized domain model"]


 The ROBOT Test for AI Output Evaluation 




Core Evaluation Criteria

[R]eliability: Are the claims, statistics, and bibliographic citations verifiable in primary databases?
[O]bjective: What are the corporate, financial, or political incentives of the platform provider?
[B]ias: How does the output reflect demographic, gender, regional, or linguistic skews from training data?
[O]wnership: Who holds intellectual property rights over the output? Were original creators compensated?
[T]ype: Is this a general foundational model, a fine-tuned domain LLM, or a retrieval-augmented (RAG) system?

title: 5. Instructional Frameworks & Evaluation Heuristics
text:
3. Lateral Reading for AI Fact-Checking
Adopted from the Stanford History Education Group (SHEG) and featured at UC Irvine, UC San Diego, and William & Mary, Lateral Reading serves as a core defense against AI hallucinations:






Vertical vs. Lateral Reading




Vertical Reading (Flawed for AI): Reading an AI output from top to bottom, judging its validity by its internal narrative flow, tone, grammar, and confident phrasing.
Lateral Reading (Recommended): Opening multiple adjacent browser tabs to independently corroborate claims, verify citations against primary databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science), and evaluate the reputation of cited sources.

Maintaining contextual continuity within a single session.

text:
5. Pedagogical Frameworks: PAIR & Bloom’s Taxonomy

The PAIR / PAIRR Framework (UC San Diego)

Problem Formulation: Defining the inquiry before touching AI.
AI Tool Selection: Choosing the right specialized tool for the task.
Interaction: Engaging in structured prompt iteration.
Reflection: Critiquing the generated output against scholarly standards.
Peer & AI Review + Reflection (PAIRR): Integrating peer feedback on AI interactions.



Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy (Auburn University)
Auburn maps GenAI tool integrations across Bloom’s cognitive levels, demonstrating where AI can act as a scaffolding tool (Remembering/Understanding) vs. where human intellectual agency must lead (Evaluating/Creating).

Student Learning Outcomes
The extracted outcomes map into two primary tiers: functional competencies (how to use tools productively) and evaluative competencies (how to critically interrogate systems).

Functional CompetenciesEvaluative & Critical Competencies



Structured Prompt Engineering

Moving beyond single-phrase search queries toward multi-parameter prompt design.
Specifying Persona/Role, Task, Context, Constraints, and Output Format (Auburn, UC Davis, UC San Diego, William & Mary).
Employing Conversational Threading for step-by-step iterative refinement.

Tool Selection for Academic Discovery

Distinguishing general consumer chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) from specialized academic discovery engines (e.g., Dimensions Research GPT, Semantic Scholar, ResearchRabbit, Elicit, Ex Libris Research Assistant).
Using seed papers to map citation networks and literature clusters (USC, Auburn, UCSB).

Responsible Coding & Technical Assistance

Using AI for debugging and code generation while retaining the ability to explain, verify, and validate every line of code (UCSB, UC Davis).





Hallucination & Citation Auditing

Interrogating synthetic text for fabricated citations, statistical errors, and non-reproducible claims.
Recognizing that database summaries are dynamic, descriptive starting points rather than primary evidence (UArkansas, William & Mary).

Algorithmic Bias & Representation

Auditing model outputs for historical, racial, gender, and Western-centric biases inherent in massive web-scraped training corpora (UC Davis, UC Irvine, UCSB).

Privacy & Data Security

Enforcing data safety: strictly avoiding the input of Personally Identifiable Information (PII), unreleased research data, or copyrighted manuscripts into public LLMs (UC Merced, UC San Diego).

Ecological & Human Labor Impacts

Understanding data center energy and water consumption, alongside global content moderation supply chains (RLHF labor) (Chapman, UC Irvine, UC Merced, UCSB).

Modeling the transparent use of AI in lesson planning, drafting case studies, and creating customized rubric criteria while maintaining human oversight (USC, UC Davis).

title: 1. Executive Summary & Typology Overview
text:
Detailed Curricular Typologies

1. Comprehensive / Balanced Hybrid (72.7%, n = 8)
Characterized by a dual-axis pedagogy that pairs operational utility (prompt engineering, iterative refinement, literature discovery) with rigorous evaluative frameworks (algorithmic bias detection, citation ethics, hallucination verification, environmental and labor cost analyses).
Institutions such as Auburn, Chapman, UC Davis, UC Merced, UC Santa Barbara, UC San Diego, USC, and William & Mary position AI literacy as an evolution of information literacy, requiring both functional capability and ethical discernment.






Hallmarks of Balanced Hybrid Guides




Teach systematic prompt construction heuristics (CLEAR, RTF, TAG).
Introduce tailored evaluation rubrics designed specifically for synthetic outputs (The ROBOT Test).
Emphasize academic integrity, attribution transparency, and citation mechanics across citation styles.





2. Tool-Use / Practical Productivity (18.2%, n = 2)
Focuses on immediate functional integration, interface navigation, and vendor-integrated library discovery platforms.
Baylor and the University of Arkansas focus on embedding GenAI within search workflows—such as natural language querying through discovery layers (e.g., Ex Libris Primo Research Assistant, EBSCO AI Insights, Mintel Leap) and research data mining scripts—while providing baseline guidance on instructor compliance and citation.


3. Critical & Ethical Evaluation (9.1%, n = 1)
Prioritizes structural critique over tool optimization.
UC Irvine centers its instructional guide on Critical Information Literacy (CIL) and the ACRL Framework, interrogating the sociopolitical dimensions of large language models (LLMs), including algorithmic bias, labor exploitation in training data pipelines, environmental impacts, and the erosion of epistemic authority.

1. Definition of AI Literacy

Explicit Definition: “AI Literacy involves understanding the functions of AI tools, ethical issues related to AI, how to use AI”

Implicit Characterization: AI literacy is characterized as a multi-dimensional capability that balances practical tool utilization (prompt engineering, AI-assisted research discovery) with critical responsibility (fact-checking, copyright compliance, ethical oversight, and academic integrity).


2. Named Instructional Frameworks

Bloom’s Taxonomy: Applied as a reference framework for instructors to evaluate and redesign course activities and learning outcomes, specifically to emphasize distinctive human skills or purposefully integrate GenAI tools as supplements to learning.



3. Objectives & Learning Outcomes
Student Learning Outcomes: - Apply effective prompt engineering techniques (assigning roles, defining audiences, specifying tone, and indicating format) to improve AI output quality - Fact-check and verify the accuracy and reliability of GenAI content before incorporating it into academic work - Properly cite and acknowledge generative AI tools in academic writing according to specific style guidelines (e.g., APA, AMA) - Utilize AI-driven discovery tools (Dimensions Research GPT, ResearchRabbit, Semantic Scholar) for literature reviews, citation analysis, and managing reading materials - Distinguish between AI, Machine Learning, and Generative AI concepts and technologies
Instructor Pedagogical Goals: - Complete professional development training such as the ‘Teaching with AI’ course - Adopt transparent syllabus policies regarding generative AI tool use using institutional options - Utilize Bloom’s Taxonomy to evaluate and adapt course activities and learning outcomes to emphasize distinctive human skills or integrate GenAI tools as learning supplements - Ensure all AI technologies used in courses undergo official institutional vetting processes


4. Policies, Permissibility & Citation

Acceptable vs. Prohibited Uses: AI use must adhere to institutional, state, federal, and international laws, guided by principles of ethics, transparency, accountability, data privacy, security, fairness, and human-centered oversight. AI tools are intended to enhance productivity and performance, but must not be used improperly, unethically, unlawfully, or insecurely. Enterprise-vetted software (such as Microsoft Copilot and Adobe Firefly) should be prioritized.
Citation & Attribution Rules: Users must cite generative AI tools whenever paraphrasing, quoting, or incorporating AI-generated content (text, image, data, etc.) into their work. Functional uses (such as editing prose or translating) should be acknowledged in a note or the text. For APA Style, unique chat URLs should be used following author-date-title-source format. AMA style guidelines suggest acknowledging AI tools in the Acknowledgements or Methods section.
Syllabus Guidelines: The Biggio Center suggests adopting one of four syllabus statements depending on the instructor’s desired level of generative AI tool use in the course. Students are expected to check course syllabi to verify whether GenAI use is permitted.

1. Definition of AI Literacy

Explicit Definition: “AI literacy is the ability to understand, use, and think critically about AI technologies and their impact on society, ethics, and everyday life.”

Implicit Characterization: AI literacy is framed as an extension of information, data, and visual literacy. It emphasizes developing ethical information behaviors, understanding the statistical/probabilistic nature of large language models, maintaining critical cognitive engagement without relying on AI as a learning shortcut, and evaluating broader societal and environmental impacts.


2. Named Instructional Frameworks

Leo Lo AI Literacy Framework: Provides the guiding definition of AI literacy, establishing that students must understand, use, and critically evaluate AI technologies and their broader societal and ethical impacts.
Ethan Mollick’s ‘Against Brain Damage’ Cognitive Learning Strategy: Used as a pedagogical heuristic to help students keep active thinking and metacognition at the center of their work, preventing AI from becoming an unthinking shortcut that short-circuits learning.
Alberto Cairo’s Data and Visual Literacy Framework (‘How Charts Lie’): Applied to teach students how to critically deconstruct data visualizations, charts, and maps to identify misleading representations and understand how data collection shapes visual narratives.



3. Objectives & Learning Outcomes
Student Learning Outcomes: - Understand foundational concepts of AI and large language models, including transformer architecture and probability-based decision-making. - Develop ethical and useful information behaviors when integrating AI tools into academic research. - Contextualize information produced by generative AI and critically evaluate potential errors or misinformation. - Maintain active human thinking and writing habits to avoid short-circuiting mental effort and deeper learning. - Evaluate the environmental impacts (energy consumption, carbon emissions, water use) of AI models and practice computational efficiency (e.g., using campus-supported PantherAI, prompt reuse). - Apply data and visual literacy skills to critically evaluate charts, maps, and statistical representations to detect deceptive or misleading data.
Instructor Pedagogical Goals: - Navigate how generative AI transforms information literacy habits and learning environments alongside students. - Provide instructional guidance that centers human critical thinking and ethical information use.


4. Policies, Permissibility & Citation

Acceptable vs. Prohibited Uses: Encourages ethical use of AI to support the research process while warning against using AI as a shortcut to replace writing and authentic thinking. Recommends questioning whether AI is necessary for a given task before use and utilizing institution-supported tools like PantherAI and Microsoft Copilot.

Acceptable vs. Prohibited Uses: Acceptable: Idea generation, getting started on drafts, refining vocabulary and grammar, writing formulaic text (e.g., emails), simplifying dense text, language translation, transcription, and acting as a non-confidential sounding board. Prohibited/Not Recommended: Using AI when prohibited by an instructor, PI, or publisher (constitutes a William & Mary Honor Code violation); generating whole papers; relying on AI for unchecked citations and bibliographies; researching rapidly evolving or real-time current events without live web access; exploring ill-defined, obscure, or non-Western topics with sparse training data; and processing sensitive, harmful, offensive, private, or confidential information.
Citation & Attribution Rules: AI tools cannot be listed as authors or co-authors because major style guides, scholarly societies, and the US Copyright Office do not recognize them as eligible for authorship. AI contributions must be explicitly acknowledged and documented. Best practices require describing the specific tool, the prompt engineering process, the version/model, the date of access, and the concrete use case (e.g., drafting, translating, editing). Authors must attribute the tool to its corporate purveyor/developer (e.g., OpenAI) and must never cite AI-generated references without independently reading and verifying the primary sources.
Syllabus Guidelines: Students must consult their specific course syllabus policies or ask their instructors directly before using GenAI, as faculty policies range from total prohibition to conditional allowance or active encouragement. Unauthorized AI use is treated as an Honor Code violation.



5. Grounded Verbatim Quotes from Source

“Being AI Literate does not mean you need to understand the advanced mechanics of AI. It means that you are actively learning about the technologies involved and that you critically approach any texts you read that concern AI, especially news articles.”
“To be AI-literate, users must constantly question and fact-check the information that Generative AI tools like ChatGPT produce. While this can be cumbersome, not exercising due diligence can have serious repercussions.”
“First check your course syllabus policies or with your professor! Some professors don’t allow it; others allow it only under specific circumstances; and others encourage it. Using it when prohibited is an honor code violation so if you’re unsure, just ask!”
“While the US Copyright Office, many journals, and a number of scholarly societies don’t consider ChatGPT eligible for authorship status, its contributions and incorporation within a work must still be acknowledged.”
“Do not use sources that are cited by AI tools without reading those sources yourself. There are two different reasons for this: Generative AI tools can create fake citations. These tools may cite a real piece of writing, but the cited content may be inaccurate.”

title: Methodology & Computational Design
text:
Step 1: Structured Extraction & Grounding Defense

1. Multi-Dimensional Extraction Schema
To prevent omission of key pedagogical features, each guide was evaluated through a structured JSON schema capturing five dimensions: - Definitions: Explicit definitions vs. implicit characterizations, definitional models. - Outcomes: Student learning outcomes vs. instructor pedagogical goals. - Policies: Permissibility spectrum, citation rules (APA, MLA, Chicago, IEEE), and syllabus templates. - Instructional Frameworks: Named models (ACRL, ROBOT, CLEAR, RTF/TAG, Bloom’s, PAIR/PAIRR). - Supporting Quotes: Direct quotes extracted from the text to substantiate every claim.


2. Verbatim Quote Verification (Fidelity Metric)
To detect and prevent model hallucinations, every extracted quote is programmatically matched against the raw text of the LibGuide:
\[\text{Fidelity Score} = \frac{\text{Verified Verbatim Quotes}}{\text{Total Extracted Quotes}}\]
If a quote cannot be located word-for-word in the source .txt, it is flagged, and the institution’s fidelity score decreases. In our primary run with gemini-3.7-flash, over 85% of quotes were matched 100% verbatim, with the remaining discrepancies originating from minor whitespace/punctuation normalization in HTML scraping.

title: Methodology & Computational Design
text:
Step 2: Vector Embeddings & Similarity Matching

1. Semantic Profile Formulation
Each institution is represented as a dense text document synthesizing its orientation, explicit definition, implicit characterization, named frameworks, student outcomes, instructor goals, and policy statements.


2. Embedding Generation
Vector embeddings are computed via gemini-embedding-2 (and verified locally via nomic-embed-text:latest in Ollama).


3. Pairwise Cosine Similarity
Pairwise similarity between two institutional embedding vectors \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) is calculated as:
\[\text{Cosine Similarity}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|_2 \|\mathbf{v}\|_2}\]
The resulting matrix is clustered hierarchically using UPGMA (Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic Mean) via seaborn.clustermap to identify latent curricular networks.

title: Methodology & Computational Design
text:
Step 3: Qualitative Thematic Synthesis
The full extracted JSON corpus alongside the nearest-neighbor similarity rankings are fed back into the LLM with a synthesis prompt acting as a lead educational researcher. The model identifies: - Thematic typologies (Balanced Hybrid, Tool-Use, Critical/Ethical). - Points of cross-institutional consensus vs. divergence. - Pedagogical explanations for nearest-neighbor pairings (e.g., why UCSB and UCSD cluster tightly at 0.969). - Actionable curricular recommendations for academic libraries.

title: 2. Definitions of AI Literacy Across Institutions
text:
Prominent Conceptual Models

1. Leo S. Lo’s Multidimensional Framework (USC & Chapman)
USC and Chapman explicitly adopt or adapt the framework developed by Leo S. Lo (2025), defining AI literacy as an ecosystemic competency:







“AI literacy goes beyond understanding AI tools; it equips individuals to critically evaluate, ethically navigate, and practically apply AI in real-world scenarios; [it is] the ability to understand, use, and think critically about AI technologies and their impact on society, ethics, and everyday life.” — USC Libraries & Chapman University LibGuides




This model establishes four interconnected pillars: - Technical Mechanics: Understanding how probabilistic models generate outputs. - Practical Application: Formulating structured prompts and integrating tools effectively. - Critical Evaluation: Auditing for hallucination, bias, and epistemic gaps. - Socio-Ethical Navigation: Navigating copyright, privacy, labor, and environmental costs.



2. Developmental Stages of Literacy (UC Santa Barbara)
UC Santa Barbara (UCSB) operationalizes AI literacy through a developmental continuum modeled directly on foundational reading and writing acquisition:







“The practice of learning how to identify, use, and evaluate AI tools and products is building a set of literacies similar to when a person learns to read, write, and think critically.” — UCSB Library

3. Cognitive Habits of Mind & Demystification (Chapman & William & Mary)
Chapman University centers its definition around cognitive habits and human metacognition:







“AI doesn’t damage our brains, but unthinking use can damage our thinking. What’s at stake isn’t our neurons but our habits of mind.” — Chapman University LibGuide




William & Mary explicitly demystifies technical gatekeeping, decoupling AI literacy from advanced computer science requirements:







“Being AI Literate does not mean you need to understand the advanced mechanics of AI… you don’t need to be a data scientist, programmer, or application developer… However, you do need to have a basic understanding of what artificial intelligence is, what it isn’t, how it works, and how to use it ethically and legally.” — William & Mary Libraries

title: 4. Institutional Guidelines, Policies, and Citation Practices
text:
Core Institutional Policy Tiers
Academic library guides recommend three primary policy models for course syllabi:

Tier 1: Prohibited UseTier 2: Conditional Use with Explicit DisclosureTier 3: Pervasive Integration



Definition: Complete restriction on all GenAI tools.
Rationale: Used in foundational courses to ensure mastery of baseline skills (e.g., introductory language acquisition, basic arithmetic, introductory prose composition).
Enforcement: Submitting AI-generated content without explicit permission constitutes academic misconduct (e.g., UCSB, William & Mary Honor Code).




Definition: Permitted for specific research and drafting phases (e.g., brainstorming, outlining, code debugging, language polish).
Requirement: Mandatory inclusion of an AI Disclosure Statement documenting tools used, model versions, prompt text, and how outputs were adapted (William & Mary, UCSD, UC Irvine).




Definition: AI tools are fully integrated into learning activities and assignments.
Pedagogy: Focuses on advanced prompt engineering, comparative AI output auditing, and prompt log reflection.

title: 4. Institutional Guidelines, Policies, and Citation Practices
text:
Citation & Attribution Standards
All 11 institutions mandate attribution whenever GenAI tools contribute to academic work. The guides synthesize the official guidance from major style manuals:








Citation Manual
Reference Entry Structure
In-Text & Methodology Disclosure




APA 7th Edition
Author: Company (e.g., OpenAI). Title: Model Name [Large language model]. URL.
Provide description of prompt and excerpt in body text or append full chat transcript. Unique chat URLs should be provided where available.


MLA 9th Edition
Title of Source: "Prompt text/description". Container: ChatGPT. Version: Date/Model. Publisher: Company. Date of Access. URL.
Acknowledge in-text when paraphrasing AI output. AI should not be listed as an author in author field.


Chicago Style
Handled primarily via notes (footnotes/endnotes) rather than bibliography: include tool name, company, access date, and prompt description.
Include prompt details in footnote or parenthetical citation. Bibliography entry discouraged unless permalink exists.


IEEE Style
Treated as private communication or unpublished non-recoverable material.
Document model, company, date, and specific prompt details in text notes.









AI Authorship Prohibition



Every surveyed library explicitly cites major academic publisher policies (Elsevier, Springer Nature, ACM, IEEE, PLOS, Taylor & Francis) stating that GenAI cannot be listed as an author or co-author on scholarly publications because non-human entities cannot take legal responsibility or intellectual accountability for manuscript integrity.

Institutions: Baylor University \(\leftrightarrow\) University of Arkansas.

Institutions: Auburn University, Chapman University, William & Mary.
Pairwise Affinity: 0.9338 – 0.9452.
Underlying Rationale: These institutions emphasize demystifying AI concepts for non-programmers, preventing cognitive offloading (“Against Brain Damage”), and implementing accessible evaluation rubrics (the ROBOT Test).
